dct_description_sm: Aerosol formation in the remote marine atmosphere and its effect on climate is expected to play an important role as a negative feedback to warmer ocean temperature.  Fine aerosols act as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and scatter incident radiation.  Arctic temperatures have increased 1.5C in two decades with consequent alterations in the duration, timing and presence of leads in the icepack.  An increase in the area of Arctic Ocean exposed to the atmosphere through open leads enhances exchange between the open water and atmosphere and may affect atmospheric dimethyl sulfide (DMS) concentrations; potentially leading to a negative feedback to Arctic warming.   The branching ratio for DMS oxidation is a function of air temperature; sulfur dioxide (SO2) formation, and therefore potentially CCN production, is enhanced as temperature increases.  Defining the branching ratio in the Arctic is difficult using conventional measurement techniques due to the ubiquitous presence of background anthropogenic SO2 and sulphate.  Isotope apportionment, which uses differences in the natural abundance of sulphur isotopes as markers of anthropogenic and biogenic sulphur, are able to resolve the contribution from each of these sources.   Do DMS mixing ratios vary with sea ice and with organic matter from the surface layer in fine aerosols?  Specifically: 1.  Does a higher incidence of open leads will result in higher atmospheric DMS mixing ratios?  2.  Is DMS sea-air transfer enhanced in the presence of organics?
dct_title_s: Dimethyl sulfide and its oxidation products during the Arctic fall (2007 and 2008)
